Degree planning

Changing your major? Compare what your credits will actually do

Changing a major changes the requirements your learning needs to satisfy. Keep your original records, build a separate audit for each target, and compare the new work left rather than only the credits a school will accept.

DegreeSteps editorial team4 min readReviewed 2026-11-01

On this page

  1. Keep one inventory and separate degree ledgers
  2. Look for valuable shifts in placement
  3. Check the requirements with the longest consequences
  4. Compare cost without hiding missing facts
  5. Use a short decision table

Put this into a plan.

Build my degree path

Keep one inventory and separate degree ledgers

Your completed course does not change its provider, identity, or original amount when you consider another degree. Its proposed placement can change. Preserve the learning record and create a school- and program-specific set of allocations.

This also protects the meaning of a confirmation. An evaluation for one major is evidence about that particular target. Ask the school how the learning will apply to the new degree rather than copying every old approval into the new requirements.

Look for valuable shifts in placement

A course that occupies elective room in one degree might satisfy the core of another. A flexible interdisciplinary degree could use learning from several subjects, while a specialized major could require a sequence you have not started. Both can be legitimate options with different purposes.

For each target, mark completed requirements, pending placements, proposed outside options, and university work still required. Do not make an unsupported course match merely to make one route look better. Leave research gaps visible so the next school conversation can resolve them.

Check the requirements with the longest consequences

Prerequisites, upper-level courses, labs, capstones, and admission to a major can control timing. A minor or concentration can also consume what initially looked like free elective space. Ask when the remaining university courses are offered and whether your proposed sequence is available.

A degree using more of your existing credit might still take longer if a required sequence starts only at certain times. Conversely, an additional course might be worthwhile if it prepares you for the career or graduate admission goal that motivated the change.

Compare cost without hiding missing facts

Use current university quotes and the same assumptions for provider study pace, fees, and records. Keep unknown charges and unconfirmed offerings explicit. A partial modeled subtotal should not be presented as the price of either complete degree.

If aid, employer support, or military benefits matter, ask how the actual program and schedule affect them. Save the baseline route so you can see what changed. Include your personal priorities, such as classroom time or a particular campus, alongside the academic totals.

Use a short decision table

Compare the two exact targets on useful completed credit, uncertain placements, new outside work, required university work, calendar constraints, and career fit. The purpose is a decision you understand, not a winner selected by one percentage.

Choose the next three answers you need from the school and pause new course purchases that depend on them. Once the evaluation is clear, keep the chosen route and its evidence together. Your inventory remains useful if your plans change again.

Sources & further reading

  • ACE: degree applicability of credit recommendations
  • College Board: degree applicability and duplicate-credit checks
  • Liberty: current residential academic policies
Use this as a starting point.

Policies and individual degree requirements can change. Confirm the exact course, catalog, and placement with the receiving school before paying for new learning.
